text: A real vector-space subset C is convex when (1-t)x+ty lies in C for x,y in C and 0<=t<=1.
provenance: Original formulation and examples of standard mathematics; independently checked from the displayed definition or calculation. Reference context: Jiri Lebl, Basic Analysis, vector spaces and convexity, https://www.jirka.org/ra/html/sec_vectorspaces.html. No source prose reproduced.

text: The convex hull of a subset A of a real vector space consists of all finite sums sum(t_i*a_i), with a_i in A, t_i>=0, and sum(t_i)=1.
provenance: Original formulation and examples of standard mathematics; independently checked from the displayed definition or calculation. Reference context: Jiri Lebl, Basic Analysis, vector spaces and convexity, https://www.jirka.org/ra/html/sec_vectorspaces.html. No source prose reproduced.

text: Any intersection of convex subsets of a real vector space is convex, because a segment joining two points in the intersection belongs to every intersected set.
provenance: Independent paraphrase checked online against Jiri Lebl, Basic Analysis, Proposition 8.1.23, https://www.jirka.org/ra/html/sec_vectorspaces.html, accessed 2026-10-13. Mathematical fact; no source prose reproduced.

text: A union of convex sets can fail to be convex: the intervals [-2,-1] and [1,2] are convex, but their union omits the midpoint 0 of -1 and 1.
provenance: Original numerical example independently checked by the midpoint calculation. Source context read online: Jiri Lebl, Basic Analysis, Exercise 8.1.13, https://www.jirka.org/ra/html/sec_vectorspaces.html, accessed 2026-10-13. No source prose reproduced.

text: The punctured plane R^2 minus {(0,0)} is connected but not convex: it contains (1,0) and (-1,0), whose midpoint is the missing origin.
provenance: Independent paraphrase and explicit midpoint check against Jiri Lebl, Basic Analysis, Section 8.1.4, https://www.jirka.org/ra/html/sec_vectorspaces.html, read online 2026-10-13. Mathematical fact; no source prose reproduced.

text: The continuous nonnegative real functions on [0,1] with integral 1 form a convex set: averaging preserves nonnegativity and the integral. They do not form a vector subspace, since the zero function is excluded.
provenance: Original explanation verified using linearity of integration and the zero-function test. Source context read online: Jiri Lebl, Basic Analysis, Example 8.1.22 and Exercise 8.1.16, https://www.jirka.org/ra/html/sec_vectorspaces.html, accessed 2026-10-13. No source prose reproduced.

text: The line {(s,1): s in R} is convex and affine, but is not a vector subspace of R^2 because it excludes (0,0).
provenance: Original coordinate example verified directly by affine combinations and the zero-vector test. Definitions read online in Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization lecture slides, Sections 2.2-2.3, https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxslides.pdf, accessed 2026-10-13. No source prose reproduced.

text: The convex hull of a set A is the smallest convex set containing A; equivalently, it is the intersection of all convex sets that contain A.
provenance: Independent paraphrase checked online against Jiri Lebl, Basic Analysis, Section 8.1.4 following Proposition 8.1.23, https://www.jirka.org/ra/html/sec_vectorspaces.html, accessed 2026-10-13. Mathematical fact; no source prose reproduced.

text: For a nonzero a in R^n and b in R, the halfspace {x: a dot x <= b} is convex. Its boundary is the hyperplane {x: a dot x = b}.
provenance: Independent formulation checked online against Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization lecture slides, Section 2.6, https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxslides.pdf, accessed 2026-10-13. Mathematical facts; no source prose reproduced.

text: For any norm on a real vector space, center c, and r>=0, the closed ball {x: ||x-c||<=r} is convex by the triangle inequality and homogeneity of the norm.
provenance: Independent formulation checked online against Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization lecture slides, Section 2.8, https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxslides.pdf, accessed 2026-10-13. The extension to any real normed vector space follows from the stated norm axioms; no source prose reproduced.

text: A polyhedron in R^n is a set defined by finitely many nonstrict linear inequalities and linear equalities. It is convex and may be empty, unbounded, or lower-dimensional.
provenance: Independent paraphrase of the definition read online in Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization lecture slides, Section 2.9, https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxslides.pdf, accessed 2026-10-13. Convexity follows by intersection; possible cases checked by x<=0 with x>=1, x>=0, and x=0. No source prose reproduced.

text: An affine map f(x)=Ax+b sends convex sets to convex sets. For convex D, the inverse image {x: f(x) in D} is also convex, even when A is not invertible.
provenance: Independent formulation checked online against Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization lecture slides, Section 2.14, https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxslides.pdf, accessed 2026-10-13. The identity f((1-t)x+ty)=(1-t)f(x)+tf(y) verifies both assertions; no source prose reproduced.

text: A nonempty convex cone K in a real vector space contains alpha*x+beta*y for every x,y in K and alpha,beta>=0. In particular, it contains 0 and is closed under addition.
provenance: Independent formulation checked online against Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization lecture slides, Section 2.5, https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxslides.pdf, accessed 2026-10-13. Nonemptiness makes the zero-vector conclusion explicit; no source prose reproduced.

text: Real symmetric positive semidefinite n-by-n matrices form a convex cone: X belongs exactly when z^T X z>=0 for every z in R^n, and nonnegative combinations preserve these inequalities.
provenance: Independent formulation checked online against Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization lecture slides, Section 2.10, https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxslides.pdf, accessed 2026-10-13. Closure verified by linearity of the quadratic form in X; no source prose reproduced.

text: Two nonempty disjoint convex sets C,D in R^n admit a nonzero a and real b with a dot x<=b for x in C and a dot y>=b for y in D. These inequalities need not be strict.
provenance: Independent paraphrase checked online against Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization lecture slides, Section 2.22, https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxslides.pdf, accessed 2026-10-13. Finite-dimensional hypotheses and weak inequalities retained; no source prose reproduced.

text: At any boundary point p of a nonempty convex set C in R^n, some nonzero a satisfies a dot x<=a dot p for every x in C. The hyperplane a dot x=a dot p supports C, even if p is not in C.
provenance: Independent paraphrase checked online against Boyd and Vandenberghe, Convex Optimization lecture slides, Section 2.23, https://web.stanford.edu/~boyd/cvxbook/bv_cvxslides.pdf, accessed 2026-10-13. Boundary-point statement does not require C to be closed; no source prose reproduced.
